subtopic_detail: Gestational ceiling for foetal neuroprotection when birth is expected within hours
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 31 year old woman in her third pregnancy at 29 weeks and 4 days. She has been contracting every three minutes for two hours, her cervix is 6 cm dilated and the membranes are intact.

She received both doses of betamethasone eight days ago during an earlier admission for threatened preterm labour. The neonatal team has been called and the cot is confirmed. Her blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, her reflexes are normal, her urine output has been 60 mL per hour, and her creatinine is within normal limits. Cardiotocography shows a normal trace. She has had no magnesium in this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 140 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Cervix 6 cm dilated, membranes intact, vertex presenting at station minus 2, contractions every three minutes
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), patellar reflexes normal, urine output 60 mL per hour, cardiotocography normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional treatment to start now?

options.text: A repeat course of intramuscular betamethasone as two doses given twenty four hours apart
options.rationale: A repeat course is considered when the first was given more than seven days earlier and birth is again threatened, but it cannot be completed in a woman delivering within hours and would delay the intervention that can be. Magnesium takes precedence when time is short. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate as a loading dose followed by an infusion until the birth
options.rationale: Antenatal magnesium given to women expected to give birth before 30 weeks reduces cerebral palsy and gross motor dysfunction in survivors, and this birth is imminent at 29 weeks and 4 days. The loading dose and infusion are started as soon as birth is anticipated rather than held back. (Source: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate withheld because the gestation has passed the threshold for neuroprotective benefit
options.rationale: The Australian threshold is birth before 30 completed weeks, and 29 weeks and 4 days sits inside it. Reading the threshold as 29 weeks or as 28 weeks is the commonest reason eligible women miss the treatment. (Source: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Intravenous nifedipine tocolysis as a loading dose followed by maintenance until 34 weeks
options.rationale: Nifedipine is an oral agent and tocolysis at 6 cm with regular contractions is very unlikely to stop labour. Its purpose is to buy time for steroids or transfer, both of which are already complete here. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour and birth)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin as a loading dose followed by four hourly doses until the birth
options.rationale: Group B streptococcal prophylaxis is reasonable in preterm labour of unknown carriage status and would usually be given, but it addresses neonatal sepsis rather than the neurological outcome that defines the window closing here. It is an addition, not the answer to what matters most now. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate given to the mother shortly before very preterm birth reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in surviving children, with a number needed to treat of roughly 60 at gestations below 30 weeks. The Australian and New Zealand guideline sets the threshold at anticipated birth before 30 completed weeks, and treatment is given as a loading dose followed by a maintenance infusion, ideally with at least four hours before birth although benefit is not abandoned if less time is available. Monitoring is clinical: respiratory rate, patellar reflexes and urine output, with the infusion stopped if toxicity appears. Normal renal function matters because magnesium is renally cleared. Steroids and neuroprotection serve different endpoints and both are given when time permits.
key_points: Neuroprotective magnesium applies to anticipated birth before 30 completed weeks
Loading dose then infusion, ideally at least four hours before birth
Monitor respiratory rate, patellar reflexes and urine output for toxicity
Renal impairment demands dose reduction because magnesium is renally cleared
Steroids reduce respiratory morbidity and do not replace neuroprotection
explanation.pearls: Loss of patellar reflexes is the earliest reliable sign of magnesium toxicity and appears well before respiratory depression, so check reflexes hourly and treat their disappearance as a reason to stop the infusion and recheck the level rather than waiting for the respiratory rate to fall below 12 breaths per minute.

sources.label: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines
RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Duration of postnatal thromboprophylaxis after caesarean in a woman with a previous unprovoked clot
stem:
You are the obstetric resident writing discharge medications for a 36 year old woman on day three after an emergency caesarean at 39 weeks for failure to progress. Her booking body mass index was 31 kg/m2.

She had an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis in her left leg at the age of 28, treated with six months of anticoagulation, and she received prophylactic enoxaparin throughout this pregnancy. Thrombophilia screening after that event was negative. Her wound is clean, she is mobilising independently, her haemoglobin is 108 g/L and her platelet count is normal. She is breastfeeding and asks how long she needs to keep having injections.

data_table.Examination: Caesarean wound clean and dry, calves soft and non tender, mobilising independently
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), platelets 244 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: How long should her postnatal thromboprophylaxis continue?

options.text: Prophylactic enoxaparin until discharge only, with graduated compression stockings continued at home
options.rationale: Stopping at discharge leaves the highest risk weeks uncovered, since most postnatal events occur after the woman goes home. Stockings are an adjunct and do not substitute for pharmacological prophylaxis in a high risk woman. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Six weeks of prophylactic enoxaparin from the day of birth, arranged before she leaves hospital
options.rationale: A previous unprovoked venous thromboembolism places her in the high risk group, for whom prophylaxis continues six weeks postnatally rather than stopping at discharge. The postnatal period carries the highest daily thrombotic risk of the whole pregnancy, and the caesarean and body mass index add to it. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.text: Six weeks of oral rivaroxaban from the day of birth, arranged before she leaves hospital
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are not recommended while breastfeeding because they are excreted in breast milk and infant safety data are lacking. Enoxaparin and warfarin are both compatible with breastfeeding. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Six weeks of therapeutic dose enoxaparin from the day of birth, arranged before she leaves hospital
options.rationale: Therapeutic dosing is for treating an acute event or for women on long term anticoagulation, not for prophylaxis after a remote treated thrombosis. It raises the risk of wound haematoma and secondary postpartum haemorrhage without added benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Ten days of prophylactic enoxaparin from the day of birth, arranged before she leaves hospital
options.rationale: Ten days covers intermediate risk, such as an emergency caesarean with one or two minor risk factors and no thrombotic history. A previous unprovoked event moves her above that band. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in Australia, and the daily risk peaks in the first postnatal weeks rather than during pregnancy. Risk is scored from a combination of previous events, thrombophilia, mode of birth, body mass index, age, parity and immobility. A previous unprovoked thrombosis is a high risk marker in its own right and mandates prophylaxis antenatally and for six weeks postnatally, while intermediate risk combinations attract ten days. Prophylaxis is with low molecular weight heparin, which does not cross into breast milk in clinically relevant amounts. Direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in breastfeeding women. The practical failure mode is not choosing the wrong drug but stopping it at discharge.
key_points: Previous unprovoked venous thromboembolism means six weeks of postnatal prophylaxis
Intermediate risk combinations attract ten days rather than six weeks
Most postnatal events occur after discharge, so the script must leave with her
Enoxaparin and warfarin are compatible with breastfeeding, direct oral agents are not
Prophylactic dosing is used even when the previous event was unprovoked
explanation.pearls: Restart low molecular weight heparin at least four hours after removal of an epidural catheter and do not remove the catheter within twelve hours of a prophylactic dose, because spinal haematoma is the complication that turns a correct prophylaxis decision into a permanent injury.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

subtopic_detail: Operative plan when imaging suggests abnormal placental invasion over a previous scar
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a tertiary maternal foetal medicine clinic reviewing a 34 year old woman at 32 weeks in her fourth pregnancy. She has had two previous caesarean sections and one vaginal birth, and this pregnancy was conceived spontaneously.

Ultrasound reports an anterior placenta reaching the internal os, with multiple placental lacunae, loss of the clear zone between placenta and myometrium, and bridging vessels crossing into the bladder wall on colour Doppler. She has had two small painless antepartum bleeds that settled without intervention. She has no pain now, the foetal growth is on the 45th centile, and she has been counselled in detail about the range of intrapartum possibilities by the consultant.

data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non tender, no vaginal bleeding today, foetus in cephalic presentation
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound showing anterior placenta praevia with multiple lacunae, loss of the clear zone and bridging vessels to the bladder, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), foetal growth on the 45th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks with the placenta left in situ, the uterus closed and methotrexate given afterwards
options.rationale: Expectant management leaving the placenta in situ is reserved for women who strongly desire uterine preservation and accept a high rate of delayed haemorrhage, sepsis and eventual hysterectomy. Methotrexate does not hasten placental involution and is not recommended as part of that strategy. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks with manual removal of the placenta and uterine artery embolisation if bleeding follows
options.rationale: Manual removal is the specific manoeuvre that converts a controlled operation into torrential haemorrhage when the villi are invading myometrium, and embolisation cannot keep pace with that rate of loss. Interventional radiology has a role in planned balloon occlusion, not as a rescue after avoidable bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks with the placenta left undisturbed and hysterectomy performed at the same operation
options.rationale: The imaging describes placenta accreta spectrum, where attempting to remove the placenta provokes catastrophic haemorrhage from vessels that cannot retract. Planned delivery before labour at a centre with the right team, with the placenta left in place and hysterectomy performed, gives the lowest maternal blood loss and morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging now, with the mode and timing of birth deferred until that result is available
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging helps define posterior placentation or the extent of parametrial spread, but it does not outperform good ultrasound for the diagnosis itself and adds nothing when the sonographic signs are this clear. Deferring the plan wastes the planning time that determines the outcome. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Planned caesarean at 39 weeks with the placenta left undisturbed and hysterectomy performed at the same operation
options.rationale: Waiting to term in a woman who has already bled twice courts an emergency delivery out of hours without the assembled team, which is the setting in which most maternal deaths from this condition occur. The gestation is deliberately traded against that risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum follows implantation over a uterine scar where decidua is deficient, so villi anchor into or through myometrium. Incidence has risen in step with the caesarean rate, and the combination of placenta praevia with previous caesareans is the classic antenatal warning. Sonographic features are lacunae, loss of the hypoechoic clear zone, myometrial thinning, and bridging vessels extending towards the bladder. Outcomes are determined almost entirely by whether the diagnosis is made antenatally and the delivery planned: a scheduled operation at 34 to 36 weeks in a centre with blood bank support, experienced surgeons and critical care halves maternal morbidity compared with emergency delivery. The operative principle is to deliver the baby through an incision away from the placenta and not to attempt separation.
key_points: Praevia plus previous caesarean is the combination that should prompt the diagnosis
Plan birth at 34 to 36 weeks before labour or a large bleed forces the issue
Deliver through an incision away from the placenta and do not attempt separation
Caesarean hysterectomy with the placenta in situ is the standard operation
Antenatal diagnosis and a planned team are the strongest predictors of outcome
explanation.pearls: Ask every woman with an anterior low placenta how many caesareans she has had, because the risk of accreta spectrum in the presence of praevia climbs from roughly 3 percent with one previous caesarean to more than 40 percent with three or more, and that single history question changes the ultrasound from routine to targeted.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

subtopic_detail: Delivery timing when serum bile acid concentration crosses the highest stillbirth risk band
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30 year old woman at 34 weeks and 3 days in her second pregnancy. For three weeks she has had intense itching of her palms and soles that keeps her awake, with no rash other than scratch marks.

Her total serum bile acids taken non fasting are 118 micromol/L, alanine aminotransferase is 96 units/L, bilirubin is normal, and a liver ultrasound, hepatitis serology and autoimmune screen are all unremarkable. Foetal growth is on the 60th centile with normal umbilical artery Dopplers and a reassuring cardiotocograph. She has been taking ursodeoxycholic acid for two weeks with modest relief of itch. Her first pregnancy ended in a normal birth at term.

data_table.Examination: Widespread excoriations on the forearms and shins, no primary rash, no jaundice, uterus soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bile acids 118 micromol/L (less than 10), alanine aminotransferase 96 units/L (5-35), bilirubin 9 micromol/L (less than 20), viral hepatitis serology negative, autoimmune screen negative, umbilical artery Dopplers normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Increase the ursodeoxycholic acid dose and defer any decision about birth until the bile acids have been rechecked
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid improves pruritus and lowers biochemistry modestly but the large randomised trial found no reduction in perinatal death, preterm birth or neonatal unit admission. Treating the number rather than the risk delays the intervention that does change outcome. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks after a course of corticosteroids, with continued inpatient foetal monitoring meanwhile
options.rationale: Stillbirth risk in this condition is concentrated in women whose bile acids reach 100 micromol/L or more, in whom the risk rises steeply from the mid thirties of gestation, so birth is brought forward to 35 to 36 weeks. Below that concentration the risk approximates background and delivery can wait until closer to term. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Repeat liver function tests and bile acids weekly and deliver only if alanine aminotransferase rises above 200 units/L
options.rationale: Transaminase level correlates poorly with perinatal risk in this condition, whereas the bile acid concentration is the variable that tracks stillbirth. Using the wrong marker as the trigger leaves an already high risk pregnancy undelivered. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Deliver by caesarean section within twenty four hours because of the height of the bile acid concentration
options.rationale: There is no evidence that abdominal birth improves outcome in this condition, and immediate delivery at 34 weeks imposes prematurity without a corresponding gain over waiting the short interval to 35 to 36 weeks. Induction is the usual route once the decision to deliver is made. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

options.text: Plan birth at 39 weeks with twice weekly cardiotocography and growth scans every two weeks until then
options.rationale: Term delivery is appropriate for mild disease but not once bile acids exceed 100 micromol/L. Surveillance is the deeper problem here: stillbirth in this condition is a sudden arrhythmic event and a normal trace does not predict the next few days. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy presents with pruritus without a primary rash, classically on the palms and soles and worse at night, and is confirmed by raised serum bile acids once other liver disease is excluded. The important shift in the last decade came from pooled individual patient data showing that stillbirth risk is not uniform across the condition: it is essentially background when bile acids are below 40 micromol/L, slightly elevated between 40 and 99, and rises sharply above 100 micromol/L, particularly after 35 weeks. Management therefore stratifies by concentration, with birth at 35 to 36 weeks for severe disease and closer to term for milder disease. Ursodeoxycholic acid remains reasonable for symptom relief but the randomised evidence shows it does not prevent perinatal death, so it must not be used as a reason to delay delivery.
key_points: Bile acids of 100 micromol/L or more define the high stillbirth risk group
Plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks for that group, later for milder disease
Ursodeoxycholic acid relieves itch but does not reduce perinatal death
Cardiotocography does not predict the sudden foetal death seen in this condition
Diagnosis requires exclusion of viral, autoimmune and structural liver disease
explanation.pearls: Take the bile acid sample non fasting, because postprandial values run higher and the risk thresholds published from the pooled data were derived largely from non fasting samples; a fasting level reported as 85 micromol/L may sit above 100 micromol/L after a meal and place the woman in a different management band.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Obstetric cholestasis

subtopic_detail: Breathlessness three weeks after birth wrongly attributed to blood loss and deconditioning
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 38 year old woman three weeks after the birth of twins by caesarean section. She describes six days of breathlessness climbing the stairs, waking at night needing to sit up, and ankle swelling that has not settled.

She lost 700 mL at operation and was told her blood count was low afterwards. Her haemoglobin today is 118 g/L, having been 104 g/L on day two. She has bilateral basal crackles, a raised jugular venous pressure and pitting oedema to mid shin, with calves that are soft and equal. Her chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly and upper lobe venous diversion, and an electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with no ischaemic change. Her blood pressure has been normal throughout the pregnancy and today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure 6 cm above the sternal angle, bilateral basal crackles, pitting oedema to mid shin, calves soft and equal, caesarean wound healed
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45-90), chest radiograph showing cardiomegaly and upper lobe venous diversion, electrocardiogram showing sinus tachycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous iron infusion with outpatient review, on the basis that her symptoms date from the operative blood loss
options.rationale: Her haemoglobin has risen from 104 to 118 g/L, so anaemia is resolving while her symptoms are worsening, and anaemia does not raise the jugular venous pressure or produce upper lobe venous diversion. Attributing postnatal breathlessness to blood loss is the commonest reason this diagnosis is delayed. (Source: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with doxycycline and discharge, treating the findings as an atypical community acquired pneumonia
options.rationale: She is afebrile with symmetrical basal crackles, oedema and a raised venous pressure, none of which fit infection, and the radiograph shows congestion rather than consolidation. Treating this as pneumonia sends home a woman in decompensated heart failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography with therapeutic enoxaparin started while awaiting the scan
options.rationale: Pulmonary embolism deserves consideration in any breathless postnatal woman, but orthopnoea, a raised venous pressure, bilateral crackles and cardiomegaly with venous diversion point to a congested circulation rather than an obstructed one. Echocardiography will answer both questions faster. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Reassurance with graded exercise and a general practice review in two weeks, treating this as postnatal deconditioning
options.rationale: Deconditioning does not cause orthopnoea, a raised venous pressure, hypoxaemia or an abnormal chest radiograph. Normalising these findings in a postnatal woman is precisely the pattern that turns a treatable cardiomyopathy into a late presentation. (Source: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines

options.text: Urgent transthoracic echocardiography with intravenous frusemide and admission under a physician
options.rationale: The clinical picture is pulmonary congestion with a raised venous pressure and radiographic changes, which requires imaging of ventricular function now and treatment of the congestion while that is arranged. Peripartum cardiomyopathy characteristically declares itself in the first month after birth and carries significant mortality if missed. (Source: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines

explanation.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is systolic heart failure arising in the last month of pregnancy or the first five months after birth in a woman with no previously known cardiac disease. Multiple pregnancy, older maternal age, hypertensive disease and multiparity all increase risk. The presentation overlaps almost completely with normal late pregnancy and early postnatal symptoms, which is why the median time to diagnosis is measured in weeks, and the discriminating features are orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, a raised jugular venous pressure and hypoxaemia. Echocardiography confirms a reduced ejection fraction and excludes valvular and pericardial causes. Treatment follows standard heart failure principles adapted for breastfeeding, using frusemide, beta blockade and an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor postnatally, with anticoagulation considered when the ejection fraction is severely reduced.
key_points: Presents from the last month of pregnancy to five months after birth
Orthopnoea and a raised jugular venous pressure separate it from deconditioning
Twins, older maternal age and hypertensive disease raise the risk
Echocardiography is the diagnostic test and should not wait for outpatient booking
Postnatal treatment uses agents compatible with breastfeeding
explanation.pearls: Captopril, enalapril and quinapril are the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors with the best breastfeeding safety data and should be chosen over perindopril or ramipril in a woman who wants to keep feeding, because being told to wean is a common reason women stop taking the drug that most improves their ejection fraction.

sources.label: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines
